item.title: Analysts find looming launch crisis is “more severe” than anticipated
item.description:
There’s no evidence that Starship will launch traditional satellites, either.

A new report from the analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years.

The firm estimatesthat between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.

“What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved,” said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. “What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s.”

The report tallies a number of familiar factors that have gone into this crisis: the war in Ukraine taking Russian rockets off the Western market; Amazon Leo demand; developmental delays in a new generation of rockets, from New Glenn and Vulcan to Neutron, Terran R, and Nova; and more recently, the retirement of the Falcon 9 as a rocket for commercial service.

At a time when the supply of commercial rockets is contracting, demand for satellite launch is soaring, from megaconstellation operators such as Amazon to a flurry of small satellite startups. The report estimates the crunch will become most acute in 2028 but should then slowly improve.

“How should people react and plan around this?” Henry asked. “To be honest, I don’t have a good answer. If you haven’t booked your launch already, and you need one, you’re late.”

Henry said several key uncertainties could change the outcome. Most importantly is what SpaceX will do. The company has intensified the shortage by winding down its prolific Falcon 9 rocket program. Starship has the potential to solve the launch crisis given its massive payload capacity and potential for rapid reuse.

But SpaceX has not been aggressively selling Starship as a commercial launch option. “SpaceX has also stopped affirming Starship as a commercial launcher,” the Quilty report states. Andas Ars reported this week, there is no evidence that the company is putting effort into developing a conventional payload fairing door for the vehicle to accommodate traditional satellites and spacecraft. Rather, the company seems set to continue to fly the vehicle with its Starlink-optimized narrow door, which ejects satellites into space like a PEZ dispenser.

SpaceX has not offered any public commitment recently to developing a larger payload fairing door, but some of its customers have indicated they don’t expect that to happen any time soon.

On Thursday, the president and chief executive of Telesat, Dan Goldberg, was asked during an earnings call about what rocket the company’s future satellites might launch on. In short, to book on Starship, the company may need to build flat satellites.

“First and foremost, they’ll focus on the deployment of their own satellites and their own requirements,” Goldberg said of SpaceX and Starship. “Secondarily or right alongside of that, the US government will be a priority customer for them, and maybe other governments as well. I do believe that so long as our next-gen satellites are configured in a way that can go into their dispenser, the same dispenser that they’ll be using to deploy their own satellites, we’ve got some expectation that Starship would be available to Telesat to support future missions.”

Another mitigating factor could be the rapid acceleration of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket launch cadence. Henry said Quilty adopted a conservative forecast, predicting eight New Glenn launches in 2028, 12 in 2029, and 16 in 2030.

“I’d be happy to be proven wrong,” he said. “And Blue has been in development for so long, they could come out of the gate swinging.”

Blue Origin, he noted, is building the production capacity for up to 150 upper stages annually, but it will of course take time to launch such a large rocket at a high rate.

A final wild card is the US military. The current phase of the national security launch program has two lanes. The first lane is for missions with a higher risk tolerance. Any company that has launched a rocket successfully a single time is eligible to bid on these missions. For now, this includes Falcon rockets, New Glenn, and United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan, but a new generation of medium-lift rockets should join within the next year or two. Lane 2 is reserved for SpaceX and United Launch Alliance.

Earlier this year, the US Space Force announced a dramatic increase in forecast demand for both Lane 1 (from an estimated 30 to 60 launches to about 170) and Lane 2 (from 54 launches to 79 launches). These missions would be ordered between 2025 and 2029.

This surge in military launch demand was not included in Quilty’s calculations, Henry said, because he believes the US military will be able to require SpaceX to perform launches it deems national priorities. Moreover, he said, SpaceX is already building a number of these satellites, such as theSpace-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicatorconstellation.

“I think the US government will compel them to do this,” Henry said. “SpaceX is already building a non-trivial number of these satellites.”

item.title: Thousands of “ghost students” use AI to steal millions in student loans, DOJ says
item.description:
Applying for FAFSA may get messy as DOJ “ghost student” crackdown ramps up.

The US has charged five individuals as part of the first broad federal crackdown on “ghost students”—fraudsters who steal the identities of hundreds of Americans to pose as fake college students and steal student loans.

In apress releaseThursday, the Department of Justice said it had uncovered a large-scale scheme relying partly on AI. The DOJ seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from “a network associated with Kenyan nationals” after data analysis helped flag likely fraudsters. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division credited new fraud-detection measures implemented by the Trump administration for the arrests. He said that “this is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya,” while warning fraudsters that the crackdown has only just begun.

“If you steal American identities, if you steal taxpayer dollars, if you exploit programs meant to help students build a future—we will find you,” McDonald said. “Whether you are in Nebraska, New Jersey, Virginia, or Nairobi, we will pursue you.”

At apress conference, McDonald was joined by FBI and Department of Education officials to explain how the scheme works.

It starts with bad actors purchasing personally identifiable information (PII) of Americans—most frequently targeting high school graduates who never attended college and went straight into the workforce.

Once they have that sensitive data, they fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) while seeking to enroll in universities and community colleges. If accepted, student aid is distributed first to schools to cover tuition and fees, but any leftover money is deposited into bank accounts controlled by the fraudsters. Dozens of Americans have opened bank accounts to act as money mules for fraudsters, the DOJ said.

To keep money flowing, bad actors use AI to fill out applications, complete coursework, and even make it appear that a student is attending virtual sessions.

“It looks like the ghost student is actually completing the class,” McDonald said at the press conference. “Some even create the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present. The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester.”

So far, the DOE has “identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts created by using this PII of US citizens,” officials said at the press conference. If all those accounts are ghost students, total losses come close to $130 million, the DOJ said.

For Americans whose data is stolen, there’s little opportunity to discover the scheme until the government comes collecting on loans years later. In the meantime, victims’ credit can be damaged. Once they detect the scheme, they’re stuck defending against demands to repay inflated student loans, which McDonald admitted is messy.

“The Department of Education does a great job to help unravel that mess, but it is a mess that no one should have to endure,” he said.

In connection with the arrests, officials said they “identified more than $32 million in actual loss tied to these specific subjects” and “we believe that actual total is substantially higher,” with “millions more suspected.”

The DOE’s Office of Inspector General first detected the fraud patterns that brought the alleged scheme to light. The FBI then helped identify how many accounts were impacted, tracing money to US and foreign bank accounts and crypto wallets. In one case, a defendant “used multiple bank accounts across several financial institutions to receive over 700 fraudulently obtained federal student aid refund deposits, totaling approximately $1,439,548,” the DOJ said. In another, “one person received more than $1 million in deposits that were linked to more than 300 fraudulent student accounts,” Inside Higher Edreported.

At the press conference, First Assistant US Attorney Theophani K. Stamos for the Eastern District of Virginia said that data analysis “identified unusual, suspicious patterns of behavior” that the FBI said indicated “coordinated fraud was happening involving FAFSA.” Those patterns gave investigators “a solid basis and a solid lead to open further inquiries that have led to indictments,” Stamos said.

To keep the crackdown going, his office has sent “approximately 50 referrals to 26 FBI field offices across the country” to hunt down stolen taxpayer funds.

“We are just getting started. Working with partners around the world, we are sending a clear message: student aid belongs to real students, the data always leaves a trail, and we will follow it wherever it leads,” Stamos said.

The DOJ suspects this scam has been running since at least 2021, growing increasingly sophisticated as AI opens new avenues for loan theft.

“These fraudsters are exploiting Americans who have never been to college before, preventing the Department of Education from cross-checking applicants,” the DOJ said. “Many known victims have reported attaining only high school diplomas—and are shocked by their faked attendance at an institution hundreds of miles away.”

At the press conference, Undersecretary of Education Nicholas Kent accused the Biden administration of leaving Americans unprotected.

“When we walked in the door last January, we were extremely troubled to find that the Biden administration had turned off nearly every fraud detection measure,” Kent said.

Trump’s DOE said it introduced online identity verification requirements that Kent claimed would stop ghost students from ever receiving funds. Relying on automated systems to flag behaviors and reject fraudulent FAFSA applications, Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, vice chair of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, insisted that fraud could be easily stopped without allocating staff and resources or overly burdening the US government.

“The computers help us find it, and we keep the money in the agency,” Ferguson said.

The automated system isn’t perfect, however, and advocates have warned that false flags burden schools, meaning students’ access to aid could be delayed as administrators work through the added identity-verification processes.

Glitches have already affected fraud detection and student applications. In August, the DOE confirmed a technical issue from June 29 to July 6 prevented fraud evaluation results from being shared with certain FAFSA forms. After detecting the glitch, the DOE reprocessed those applications.

Colleges and universities are also considering adding fees to stop the ghost student fraud.

Some advocates have acknowledged that the fraud deprives real students of funds. But they’re concerned that both the fees and online identity verification could become barriers to access to higher education for low-income students.

To verify their identities through the online FAFSA portal, students are expected to have government-issued IDs on hand in “real time.” They hold the IDs up to their cameras, and automated systems review them. A senior DOE officialtold Insider Higher Edthat the systems are “similar to the ones used by financial services companies like banks” and that he believed they are the same ones used by rental car companies.

Automated systems then assign a risk rating to the student, and anyone flagged as “high risk” is rejected. Once a student is rejected for aid, it’s up to the university to conduct any follow-up to verify if the application was real.

MorraLee Keller, a senior consultant for the National College Attainment Network, told Inside Higher Ed that “a lot of low-economic kids may not have secured, for example, a driver’s license” and may be set back in the application process while trying to obtain alternative IDs. That could also add fees during the application process.

Students may also be subject to automated fraud detection when seeking to make corrections to their FAFSA, which could delay fund distribution if a false rejection is issued.

“We want to make sure that timing doesn’t interrupt the aid getting credited to their account to pay their bills on time so that they could start classes, get refunds to go get their books, and all those kinds of things,” Keller said.

The Trump administration has said that it expects the number of real students flagged as fraudulent to be low. But the president of the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators, Melanie Storey, pushed back “a little bit” on that claim during a podcast from the association recently, asking “the department to quantify the volume of in-person verification that will remain,” Inside Higher Edreportedin April. At the time, Aaron Lemon-Strauss, executive director of the FAFSA program, replied, “I’m not going to be able to give you a number yet.”

Storey noted that many people complete the FAFSA form at in-person events, further narrowing potential false positives as the government expands its ghost student crackdown. For any students who “accidentally get caught in the net,” Lemon-Strauss recommended that universities remain vigilant and take action to ensure support goes to Americans who need it most.

item.title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
item.description:
Low costs and offline security mean magnetic tape still has a job.

In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape.

Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing “exponential growth” in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels.

The investment in Fujifilm’s Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it “the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities.” The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation “FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10” tape.

Mainstream consumers may have abandoned tape decades ago, but the enterprise world never did. Cloud giants rely on tape to back up vast troves of data. Fujifilm’s work with magnetic tape as a data storage medium dates back to the 1950s, and in 2000, the company released its first LTO Ultrium storage tape. In 2011, the company was the first to commercially produce tape with barium ferrite magnetic particles, and in 2025 it debuted the LTO Ultrium10, the first storage solution in the medium to use what the company calls “fine hybrid magnetic particles” by combining barium ferrite with strontium ferrite tech. Each generation of tape (currently Gen 10) has seen meaningful increases in both compressed and uncompressed storage limits.

According to Fujifilm, “major cloud service and data center operators” have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. Fujifilm highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data: “Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware.”

item.title: Rare meteorite from Mars gives us a view into its ancient crust
item.description:
A meteorite found in the Sahara is a rare piece of Mars’ ancient crust.

Crater counts tell us that most of the Martian surface is more than 3 billion years old, but pieces of Mars we have on Earth tell a different story. The three main classes of Martian meteorites—shergottites, nakhlites, and chassignites—are all 2.4 billion years old or younger. Until now, only two genuinely ancient Martian meteorites were known: Allan Hills 84001, found in Antarctica, and a jumbled rock from northwest Africa nicknamed Black Beauty. Now we have a third one.

A team led by Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, has shown that a Martian meteorite called Teghaza 001, found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022, formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. “It’s very old and similar to some of the oldest rocks on Earth,” Liu says.

“We don’t fully understand why old Martian rocks are so rare on Earth,” Liu said. Part of the answer may lie in how a piece of Mars gets here. It takes a large impact to launch a rock off the planet, and not every rock can survive that. “If the impact hits into loose powder, it may not get cemented to become a rock and fly off Mars’ gravity,” Liu said. “So the natural impact already acts as a filter. Weak rocks do not make it off Mars.”

That left scientists with a biased collection.

“Even to date, none of our collected Martian meteorites are similar to what we found on the surface,” Liu said. The partial exception is Black Beauty, which has a bulk chemistry that matches orbital measurements. But Black Beauty is a mix of soil and many small rock fragments. Teghaza 001 is a single, intact igneous rock.

Teghaza 001 was acquired through the desert meteorite trade, where hunters comb the Sahara for dark stones that stand out against the sand. Its eight stones, weighing just under 800 grams in total, were bought by a private collector, who sent a piece to the University of New Mexico for classification. There, planetary scientists Carl Agee and Karen Ziegler measured its oxygen isotopes. “Each planetary body has a very characteristic oxygen isotope value,” Liu says. Teghaza 001’s values matched those of other Martian meteorites.

At first, the rock was classified as a shergottite, the most common (and young) type of Martian meteorite. But Agee noticed some oddities and reached out to Liu. One of Teghaza’s minerals had been altered on the inside while its outer part stayed pristine, the reverse of how weathering on Earth works. The oxygen isotopes looked a bit strange, and there was some manganese-rich material similar to what Liu had studied in Black Beauty.

“When I got to the sample, I looked around, I said, ‘That’s boring,’” Liu said. “The high-manganese material is actually terrestrial, but I quickly realized the sample is very different, very special.”

Teghaza 001 is made mostly of feldspar, a pale mineral common in the crusts of rocky planets. It has darker pyroxene crystals mixed in; according to Liu, those resemble some rocks exposed in the lunar highlands. Its crystals are rather big, up to a millimeter across, which scientists interpret as an indication it cooled down slowly. “For slow-cooled rock, they tend to have time to grow bigger,” Liu said.

By comparing the crystals with lab experiments and terrestrial rocks, the team estimated Teghaza 001 cooled by roughly 0.01° Celsius per year, indicating it formed from magma that never erupted but instead solidified inside the crust.

The team dated the rock in several independent ways. Zircon grains gave about 4.11 billion years. Phosphate minerals and rubidium-strontium dating gave similar ages. “Doesn’t matter what type of zircon we are analyzing or what mineral we are analyzing, we get this very consistent age. And we didn’t expect that,” Liu said.

It is notoriously hard to reset the age of zircons, and the impact that launched the rock, while strong enough to forge high-pressure minerals, wasn’t hot enough to do it. “To change it, you really require some kind of hydrothermal fluid,” Liu said.

Sodium-rich rims on feldspar grains and sodium trapped in the zircons support the idea that hot water percolated through the rock shortly after it formed. So 4.1 billion years marks its last soaking, the youngest of what were probably several alteration events. “The crystallization age would be older than 4.1 billion years,” Liu said.

Teghaza 001 is also unusually rich in oxygen-18, a heavier form of oxygen, with about two parts per thousand more than other Martian meteorites. Neither crystallization nor gas escaping from magma can produce a difference that big. Because water that reacts with rock at low temperatures near the planet’s surface forms minerals rich in heavy oxygen, the team thinks the magma either swallowed bits of crust that had already interacted with surface water or reacted directly with fluids that had picked up the same heavy signature.

This implies that “There was active circulation of water through Martian crust,” Liu said. “When this rock was forming, we do have a hydrosphere on Mars, and that hydrosphere is reacting with Martian crust intensely.” The water must have been circulating through the crust and reacting with magma before it had even finished cooling. “It’s actually more dynamic and more active than we thought,” Liu said. She argues that this finding fits the picture of a wet early Mars and points to potentially habitable environments in its crust.

Teghaza 001 also reveals details about Mars’ interior. The rock crystallized near the surface, but the magma it formed from came from much deeper. Ratios of trace elements that resist alteration, like the zirconium to titanium ratio, differ from those in every other Martian meteorite. The team’s melting models matched the rock’s chemistry best when its mantle source contained garnet, a mineral that is stable in the Martian mantle only at depths of more than 160 kilometers.

Studies of other Martian meteorites suggest that as an early ocean of magma solidified on Mars roughly 4.5 billion years ago, the mantle separated into three to five reservoirs. Teghaza 001’s source does not match any of them. “In the first few hundred million years, the Martian mantle was evolving in a way that’s more complicated than we thought,” Liu said.

Comparing the rock’s chemistry with orbital maps, the team suggests it most likely came from the southern highlands, northwest of the giant Hellas impact basin. “No matter how many meteorite samples we have, we will always have this question: Where are they coming from on Mars?” Liu said.

Orbital data can narrow a source down to a patch of roughly 100 by 100 meters at best, which often amounts to one pixel in our remote sensing data. When Teghaza 001 left Mars is also an open question. “We only did the minimum required to make the world know this sample is special,” Liu said, adding that two or three groups are already studying it to get further insights.

The real game-changer, Liu said, would be samples collected with careful geological context, like those Perseverance has gathered in and around Jezero Crater. Liu would like to see some from terrains as old as Teghaza 001 or older. “If these samples come back, there are so many discoveries that can be made,” Liu said. “This could revolutionize our understanding of Mars and the early solar system.”

Liu’s study on Teghaza 001 is published in Science:https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adz5646

item.title: Basically no one is using AI agents for their DoorDash orders
item.description:
But it’s still early days for the relatively new e-commerce use case.

As AI tools and agents have continued their march across all aspects of digital life,many companiesaretrying to use LLMstoimprove the experienceofpurchasing goods and serviceson the Internet. Thus far, though, a vanishingly small number of people seem to be taking advantage of those capabilities, at least when it comes to using the popular food delivery app DoorDash with an outside AI agent.

Ina third-quarter earnings call Thursday, DoorDash co-founder and CEO Tony Xu responded to an analyst question by noting that “AI agents are generating several hundred orders [on DoorDash] across the time that they’ve been up and running.” In a marked understatement, Xu called this a “very low use case” for a company that handled just shy of 1 billion orders total in the third quarter of 2026 alone.

Speaking generally, Xu said he sees the potential for AI agents to be genuinely helpful for “long consideration purchases” and major decisions where agents would be “doing work on your behalf proactively in the background.” However, Xu added, “when it comes to a task that’s as simple as ordering food, we tend to see that come directly to DoorDash.”

To be fair to the AI boosters, DoorDash only rolled out its Model Context Protocol (MCP) connectorless than a month ago. The connector provides a standardized, open-standard way for third-party AI tools to easily order through DoorDash’s platform. Without that kind of linkup—which is still only available to a small number of “early beta partners” and mainly used to streamline corporate lunch orders—AI agents have to go through a bit more effort to access DoorDash through a web interface, for instance.

Xu’s discussion of “third-party agent” orders also doesn’t include DoorDash’s own internal AI tools. Those include an “Ask DoorDash” feature the companyrolled out this summerthat can, for instance, create an online shopping cart from a photograph of a recipe or suggest an order based on a vague description like “dinner for a family of four.”

DoorDash hasn’t shared detailed statistics on that kind of usage, but the companysaid last monththat Ask DoorDash baskets get built “five times faster” than those built without, and Ask DoorDash orders “average nearly 50% higher basket value and about 60% more unique items than the same consumers’ traditional orders.” The company also said nearly half of Ask DoorDash orders end up at “local spots the consumer has never tried before,” helping with discovery of new area restaurants.

That’s all to say that DoorDash’s current experience with agentic ordering may be a bit likePizza Hut’s first tentative online ordering experiments in 1994. Back then, it would have been hard to picture today’s world, where more than half of Pizza Hut orders are placed online.

Maybe ordering food and other goods using AI agents will be just as commonplace years from now, and we’ll look back at these early statistics with bemusement. For now, though, Xu at least seems relatively cool on the early numbers.

“My take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity,” he said regarding AI agents. “But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional.”

item.title: Over 25% of people lie to get antibiotics—and their lies aren’t even good
item.description:
Faked symptoms still point to infections that antibiotics don’t treat.

A significant number of patients in the US lie to their doctors to get antibiotics they likely don’t need, according to two new studies. While that may not be a startling revelation, the studies drills down on the phenomenon, finding that the lies patients tell are generally bad ones—and yet, they work almost all the time.

In thetwolinkedstudiespublished Friday in JAMA Network Open, a team of researchers led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah analyzed online survey data from over 1,000 adults. They found that over a quarter of people reported having lied to a clinician at least once to get an antibiotic prescription for themselves or a child in their care. Patients lied by either exaggerating symptoms, making up symptoms, or—most often—both.

But interestingly, the lies people told to get antibiotics involved making up or exaggerating symptoms of infections that wouldn’t be treated with antibiotics. For example, the most common falsehoods were symptoms associated with colds, such as fever, cough, and sore throat. That’s despite the fact that colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria—which antibiotics treat.

Further, while the data suggests many patients were being dishonest, clinicians responded with what could be considered their own form of dishonesty; in most cases, the dubious fibs led to antibiotic prescriptions. Specifically, 77 percent of adult patients and 87 percent of caregivers said their lies worked, leading them to get the antibiotic prescriptions they wanted.

“These findings signal a significant issue for health professionals making antibiotic prescribing decisions and for the fields of antimicrobial stewardship and public health,” Thorpe and colleagues concluded.

For the study, the researchers reviewed survey responses from 1,371 online respondents and found 959 responses that were valid and complete. Of those, 268 (28 percent) respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms to get antibiotics. Of those, 108 reported exaggerating symptoms, 19 reported fabricating symptoms, and 141 reported doing both. In a separate analysis of 263 respondents who identified as caregivers, 63 (27 percent) reported misrepresenting symptoms of a child to get antibiotics.

The most common reported reasons for lying were that people: felt their illness or the illness of a child in their care was particularly severe; believed that antibiotics were the only thing that would help them; believed antibiotics would help them return to responsibilities (work/school) faster; or felt they should have personal autonomy (thinking they know more about their health status than the clinician or feeling like they should get to decide their own treatment).

Those who misrepresented their symptoms tended to be younger and feel their symptoms were not taken seriously by clinicians. They were more likely to believe that antibiotic resistance is a hoax, such as a scare tactic by the government or a gimmick by drug companies to justify charging more for antibiotics. People who lied were also more likely to have more underlying conditions, view lying as more acceptable, and report needing help reading health-related materials. On the other hand, those who didn’t report misrepresenting their symptoms tended to have greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics.

For people who reported misrepresenting symptoms, the online survey gave them additional questions about the types of symptoms they fabricated or exaggerated. The most common falsehoods, reported by 65 percent of dishonest patients, were to misrepresent cold-related symptoms. After that were misrepresented stomach symptoms (49 percent), joint or muscle pain (46 percent), eye symptoms (34 percent), rashes and other skin conditions (32.5 percent), urinary symptoms (31 percent), or a general feeling of being unwell (37 percent). Respondents could also report not remembering what they lied about.

“To be clear, none of these are specific indications for antibiotics,” Jeffrey Linder, of Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, wrote inan accompanying commentary, highlighting that these lies shouldn’t have helped patients get unnecessary antibiotics. “In fact, of the 8 categories offered that patients could have exaggerated or made up to get antibiotics, only 1 of them (urinary symptoms) clearly justified antibiotic prescribing,” he wrote.

While symptoms of respiratory infections can be due to bacterial infections in some situations—namely, acute sinus infection, strep throat, or pneumonia—those conditions have specific clinical guidance and/or associated tests to confirm the diagnosis, Linder highlights.

Given the magnitude of the deception, the findings raise concern that the ill-gotten antibiotics could contribute to the rise of antibiotic-resistant infections. Misuse and overuse of antibiotics are known todrive the development and spread of drug resistance. This week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention releasedan updated report on antimicrobial resistance threats, finding that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi are now causing 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths in the US each year.

But in the accompanying commentary, Linder said that an even more concerning consequence may be the “erosion of trust” between clinicians and patients. Linder acknowledged that drug resistance is a concern, but said that on the basis of an individual patient, in most clinical circumstances, the development of drug resistance is “probably irrelevant.”

To Linder, the more pertinent question doctors must face is: “Is this prescription more likely to help my patient or hurt them?” The answer is that it’s more likely to hurt; unnecessary antibiotics provide no benefit, but pose risk of adverse events, allergic reactions, and disruption of healthy microbiomes, which can provide an opening for opportunistic pathogens, such asClostridioides difficile(which is classified as a “serious threat” in the CDC’s newly updated antimicrobial resistance threat report.)

“For these non-antibiotic-appropriate diagnoses, prescribing antibiotics is medically incorrect and could itself be considered a form of dishonesty or lying mainly to assuage the patient,” Linder wrote. That dishonesty is corrosive, he said, quoting philosopher Sissela Bok, who wrote extensively about lying and, even specifically, about lying to get antibiotics. In 1978, Bok noted that antibiotics are “sometimes used as placebos” and many parents “come to believe that they must ask for the prescription of antibiotics every time their child has a fever or a cold.” But Bok argued that when clinicians prescribe medications more likely to harm than help, such “practices lacking in candor” threaten “the entire institution of medicine.”

Linder concludes by reminding readers that “Clinicians’ obligation is to act in patients’ best interest, even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms.”

Thorpe and colleagues, meanwhile, conclude with a call to address the reasons patients lie in the first place, writing: “Strategies to improve communication about antibiotics are needed to address patient concerns, support understanding of appropriate antibiotic use, and strengthen patient-clinician relationships.”

item.title: Dartmouth’s provost warned us about AI cheating—but his own AI use cost him his job
item.description:
People who love AI don’t always love telling others they used it.

On August 9, 2026, Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell wrote aWashington Post op-edcalled “Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem.” This week, Schnell discovered the depths of the problem himself as he resigned from the university after an advisory committeefoundthat he failed to disclose significant AI use in an academic paper and in the Washington Post op-ed, even though publishers required such disclosure.

Schnell didn’t make it especially easy for the committee to investigate his AI use; the report uses the term “insufficient cooperation.” He did turn over his Dartmouth laptop, but he did not turn over logs from his personal LLM accounts related to the writings in question. Nor did he agree to meet with the committee.

The committee did get access to the Claude enterprise account Schnell had used through Dartmouth, though. This shows him using the LLM as a tool for revising his papers, finding and fixing bugs in code, and editing or generating figures. For instance, Schnell would run his papers through Claude and ask things like:

I am getting read[y] to submit the enclosed paper, its supplementary materials and the enclosed repo to ChemSystemsChem. This paper is not biological, but rather chemical. Imagine that you are a reviewer for this paper with expertise in nonlinear chemical dynamics and mathematical chemical kinetics. What would be your referee report for this paper?

This is quite a bit different from asking Claude to write your entire paper for you, and Schnell has long insisted that he used AI as an editorial aid and discussion partner. He told Semafor that he had used chatbots “to refine a few arguments” and “check for grammatical errors.” He told one journal editor that he “used AI as an editorial tool” to “help refine sentences, improve clarity, and the expression of arguments.” He had not disclosed his AI use to an academic journal, he said, because he “did not understand that this type of AI-assisted editing required disclosure.”

Indeed, Schnell’s own description of what he did with AI doesn’t sound, on the long list of AI-powered sins, like it would rank near the top. But it’s hard to know. As the Dartmouth committee points out, the full scope of Schnell’s AI use was unclear to them. The committee believes that Schnell’s public statements may understate “the nature of the Provost’s actual AI use” and says that Schnell regularly “went beyond his other public descriptions of his use of AI in writing.”

We do know that Schnell also asked LLMs to takeTeX filesand “make the corrections to the files, and the repo. If you have to generate new figures, please provide them to me. Let me know what you change in the repo, and text files so that I can take a look into it.”

Whatever you think of his actions, Schnell repeatedly failed to disclose them. It is certainly possible that he thought his AI use was on par with a spelling or grammar checker, though one Claude exchange raises questions about whether Schnell wanted to hide traces of LLM activity in his work. From the committee report:

Provost Schnell’s Claude logs reflect that he uploaded to Claude a manuscript of a forthcoming article entitledAcademic Freedom and Catholic Mission: The Procedural Overlap Zone in University Governanceand prompted Claude: “Are there many signatures of AI writing in this article?” Schnell later submitted a revised manuscript that incorporated the kinds of changes Claude suggested.

Schnell has now resigned. Dartmouth, though, is barreling ahead with AI. The university calls itself the place that “launched the field of artificial intelligence” back in 1956, when “the term was coined and the foundational question was asked: Can machines solve problems once reserved for human minds?” Seventy years later, Dartmouth ishosting a conferencecalled “What Must Remain Human?” that will feature a student hackathon sponsored by Anthropic and speakers like Mira Murati and Yann LeCun.

Despite the scandal, Dartmouth President Sian Leah Beilock wants more AI. (She wrote apiece for The Atlanticin September called “Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth.”) What’s crucial, though, is that the school’s leaders should “hold themselves to the highest standards,” she said. This appears to mean one main thing: disclosure.

Inannouncing Schnell’s resignation, Beilock wrote that “each of us brings a different perspective on how and when to incorporate AI into our work and our lives. Moreover, keeping Dartmouth at the forefront of AI inevitably means leading through an environment that is fluid and fast-changing. That is why, as leaders, it is so critical that we model the transparency and human judgment that we expect from our students and scholars.”

What does “disclosure” mean? In aSeptember 2026 paperon AI detection tools, called “Who Wrote This?”, Schnell himself goes to great lengths to argue that “human-written” or “AI-written” is far too simple a binary. In his view, everything will become a mix of human judgment and AI work, and there’s nothing wrong with that. The key for him is that the human author takes full responsibility for the text, however it was composed and edited.

In the paper, Schnell lays out his method for producing it. It’s worth quoting at some length:

In September 2026, I asked OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Pro whether an AI-written essay could ever be identified with certainty, and I suggested connecting the problem to Turing’s imitation game and to the “reverse” Turing test posed by AI-text detection. GPT-5.6 Pro connected the question to binary hypothesis testing and statistical decision theory, proposed early structures and titles, identified candidate literature, and generated portions of early drafts. I chose the problem, journal, audience, and eventual direction of the argument. I decided which examples and results should remain central, including the decision to retain the Liang study while confronting it with important counterevidence. I checked the cited literature, rejected or corrected claims that I judged inaccurate, corrected mathematical and conceptual errors, and reorganized the argument.

In revising the manuscript, I rewrote most sections and added substantial explanations. I occasionally asked GPT-5.6 Sol to provide language-editing assistance for sections I had rewritten. I created the figures and made the final decisions about the mathematics, interpretation, sources, organization, and wording. I take full responsibility for the resulting manuscript.

Before submitting the manuscript for publication, I also asked GPT-5.6 Pro and Anthropic Claude Fable 5.1 to review it critically and identify issues that reviewers might raise. I evaluated the issues they identified and made corrections where I judged them warranted.

Despite all this assistance, Schnell resists the idea that AI is a “co-author.” Instead, he writes, “Calling [the paper] ‘coauthored’ would introduce a different confusion. Mathematical tools have long made substantive contributions without thereby becoming authors… The point is not that the software contributed nothing. It is that contribution and authorship are different roles.”

He is not against disclosure, as he makes clear by describing his method. Yet curiously, when submitting other papers for publication, he did not disclose his AI use even when required by publishers.

Confused about the rules in an age where even universities are pushing AI? So are many students.New survey dataunveiled at this weekend’s conference shows that 61 percent of college students think AI helps explain difficult concepts, and half believe that they produce better work after talking through issues with AI tools. But “70 percent of the college students in the survey indicate that take-home work has become unfair due to AI, with 39 percent feeling pressured to use it because their peers do.” Among Dartmouth students, 92 percent of them fear “that AI can hurt writing skills.” And many of them believe their peers are using far more AI than they actually are.

Not everyone is racked with existential doubt over how to deal with AI, though. Dartmouth student Eli Moysewrote in a September op-edthat Schnell should be fired because “a fetishization of AI to earn publicity for the College has rotted the brain of our top academic.”

item.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
item.description:
It’s still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic’s verified Cursor account.

An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers’ machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident.

The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the companysaidFriday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor,according toindependent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account.

“It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more detailshere.

Anthropic has yet to issue public notice of the incident to customers.

Cursor said that the malicious extension attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor using an added attacker-controlled SSH key, enabling the local SSH service, and opening a reverse SSH tunnel. The code was written to work on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Because Cursor extensions run with the permissions of the tool’s Integrated Development Environment, the backdoored version likely would gain access to local files, source code, and developer tooling once it was installed.

Cursor said the capabilities of the backdoor include:

Phorion said the theft of variable names allowed the operator to quickly take inventory of cloud credentials and API tokens stored on a compromised device, likely so it could prioritize which machines to target in follow-up attacks.

Bugs in the malicious code for Windows and macOS prevented the backdoor from working in some cases. Phorion said that despite the coding flaws, “the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.”

Cursor said company personnel worked with the cloud provider hosting the server the reverse shell connected to so that infected devices could no longer reach it. Personnel also removed the backdoored version from the marketplace and blocked further distribution. The company also shut down the VSCode Marketplace to rotate keys, audit access controls, and confirm no other extensions were compromised. The marketplace is now open.

It remains unclear why Anthropic isn’t publicly warning customers of the threat and why it and Cursor aren’t explaining how the supply-chain compromise happened. Neither company answered questions seeking this information.

Anyone who installed or updated Anthropic’s VS Code extension from Cursor between 5:27 am ET and 4:35 pm on Thursday should consider themselves affected, although it may be wise for anyone who has recently done so to also consider themselves potentially infected. Both Cursor and Phorion list various indicators of compromise, including IP addresses and cryptographic hashes.

item.title: Supersonic airliner in doubt as company shifts to powering AI data centers
item.description:
Boom’s airliner may be delayed, and its data center power business lost a customer.

Boom Supersonic CEO Blake Scholl recently declared “it’s time for a renaissance in energy and in supersonic flight” as the supersonic airliner company unveiled a Colorado factory dedicated to making gas turbines for AI data centers. But Boom may be facing turbulence after early backers for both ventures have questioned the company’s delivery timeline or backed out entirely.

One of the company’s first customers, United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, has expressed doubts about Boom’s original plan to deliver the first Overture supersonic airliner in 2029. Kirby’s latest frank assessment came during an interview with theOffice Hours: Business Editionpodcast that appeared on October 28, 2026.

“‘29 is their official timeline,” Kirby told podcast host Monica Langley. “It’s not going to happen in ‘29—it’s going to take longer.”

Boom first made headlines for flying its XB-1 demonstrator aircraft in 2024 and 2025 to demonstrate a “boomless cruise” concept that harnesses theMach cutoffphenomenon. Such a feat involves flying just beyond supersonic speeds at higher altitudes under specific atmospheric conditions, so that the aircraft’s shockwaves refract upward and minimize the impact on the ground.

The company’s plan to revive supersonic air travel has been backed by the Trump administration via efforts to ease regulations. In June 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposed a new ruleoverturning a long-standing banon commercial supersonic flights over the United States, following anexecutive orderfrom President Donald Trump.

Boom’spressreleaseshave previously described achieving aircraft certification and carrying the first paying customers by 2029. The company has conditional agreements with American Airlines, Japan Airlines, and United Airlines involving non-refundable deposits of unknown amounts that would allow the airlines to fully purchase the Overture aircraft once it becomes commercially available.

But United CEO Kirby pointed out that Boom still has “a lot of hurdles to overcome” while developing Overture and getting the supersonic airliner certified by the FAA. “So it’s not a guarantee that they’ll overcome,” he cautioned during the podcast interview, even though he praised Scholl and the company in general.

This follows Kirby’searlier commentsback in March that put the chances of Boom’s Overture airliner entering commercial service at “50-50.” Ars has reached out to Boom for comment.

Although Boom completed building the factory intended for production of the Overture airliner in 2024, the facility located at Piedmont Triad International Airport in Greensboro, North Carolina, has mostly sat dormant since that time. That hasraised questionsfor North Carolina state leaders who provided more than $50 million in taxpayer funding to help build the Overture factory.

Since October 2025, NASA has separately been doing test flights involving theexperimental X-59with a long, needle-like nose designed to reduce the sonic booms from supersonic flight. But this is a completely different approach than Boom’s use of the Mach cutoff flights.

Much of Boom’s recent focus has been on developing natural gas turbines to power AI data centers as an additional revenue stream. On October 22, the companyunveiled another factoryin Centennial, Colorado, dedicated to producing a 42-megawatt natural gas turbine called Superpower for data centers.

The Trump administration’s public support of Boom was once again evident as US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright participated in the event alongside Colorado Governor Jared Polis.

Boom described its new Superpower factory as making turbine parts while still undergoing construction. It aims to deliver the first gas turbines to AI data center customers in mid-2027 while ramping up annual production to 25 turbines in 2028 and 50 turbines by 2029.

Boom’s detour into powering data centers coincides with many tech companiesprioritizing natural gasas the primary power source to get their projects up and running. Some data center developers are even using “mobile gas generators strapped to semitrucks” or “aeroderivative turbines originally designed for aircraft and warships,” according to themarket intelligence platform Cleanview.

However, Boom CEO Scholl alsoacknowledged the recent lossof a $1.25 billion deal that would have seen data center developer Crusoe purchase 29 of Boom’s gas turbines,in a poston the social media platform X on September 25. Crusoe has been involved in buildingTexas data centersforOracle,GoogleandMicrosoftthat draw upon various power sources including natural gas and renewables.

Scholl said Boom “will be delivering about 250MW of Superpowers next year to other sites” but did not specify theAI data centercustomers that may be using the gas turbines.

Still, Boom has characterized the development of a gas turbine for data centers as being synergistic with its design of the Symphony engine for the Overture airliner. During the October announcement, it also described having completed a prototype turbine core, called Sprint Core, that is intended to eventually power both the Superpower gas turbine and Symphony engine for the airliner.

That turbine core is set to undergo testing at the Colorado Air & Space Port, with Boom planning to fire the turbine for the first time before Thanksgiving. That would be a concrete development milestone, but the company still has much to do in proving it can get both its AI data center and supersonic airliner ventures off the ground.

item.title: Oh captain, our captain: Ars staff remembers Patrick Stewart
item.description:
“For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard. … We created an admirable individual.”

Along with the rest of the world, we at Ars are mourningSir Patrick Stewart—the beloved award-winning actor best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard inStar Trek: The Next Generationand Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise—whodied yesterdayat the age of 86.

A statement released by Stewart’s representatives said:

We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.

Through the actor’sX account, the family has requested that, in lieu of flowers, memorial contributions be made to theJohns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fundand theAlzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources.

Born in Yorkshire, England, in 1940, the acting bug bit Stewart at the age of 12, when his English teacher handed out scripts for Shakespeare’sThe Merchant of Veniceand asked young Patrick to read the part of Shylock—a role the adult Stewart would later play for the Royal Shakespeare Theater (RSC), among many other parts. His signature bald head emerged early, around 19, thanks to alopecia. He briefly worked as a cub reporter and a furniture salesman before winning a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theater School, and he landed his first professional role in 1959, playing a marooned pirate in a production of Treasure Island for the Lincoln Repertory Company.

Stewart worked regularly in theater and on British television, and his big break came in his late 40s. The actor was conducting master classes on Shakespeare at the University of California, Los Angeles, when a TV producer developingTNGheard him lecture and thought he would make a perfect captain for theEnterprise-D. Creator Gene Roddenberry wasn’t initially keen on the choice, but Stewart’s audition changed his mind. The rest is television history.

OnInstagram, fellow thespian Sir Ian McKellen—who first met Stewart when both were young actors with the RSC and co-starred as Magneto in the X-Men films—recalled the day Stewart told him about the Star Trek offer.

“’But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK,'” McKellen recalled saying. “‘Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?’ Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did.”

Stewart himself never expressed anything but pride in the role. “For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that’s fine,” he told The Independent in 2003. “I really believe we created an admirable individual.”

TNGended in 1994, but it wasn’t long before Stewart created another iconic role, starring as Professor Charles Xavier in 2000’sX-Men, alongside McKellen as Magneto. He reprised the role in six more films and voiced the character in multiple video games.

He was a serious actor who never took himself too seriously, relishing Shakespeare, Ibsen, and Beckett but also throwing himself into comedic TV appearances onSaturday Night Live, The Daily Show(he was a “special correspondent” for several segments in 2012), andSesame Street. Who could forget his timeless “Soliloquy on B,” channeling Hamlet? Or his daily readings ofShakespearean sonnetsthat helped us all get through the COVID-19 pandemic? He voiced Napoleon in 1999’sAnimal Farm, CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock onAmerican Dadand, earlier this year, Sir Nitchfield in the delightfulSheep Detectives.

In between acting gigs, Stewart found time for charity work, advocating for such causes as domestic violence prevention and PTSD awareness among members of the armed forces, drawing on his own childhood being raised by an abusive father. All of this made Stewart one of the most beloved actors of our time. Tributes to Stewart are all over social media today, as celebrities and regular folk alike reflect on everything the actor’s work has meant to them over the years, includingthese heartfelt wordsfrom his lifelong friend McKellen:

Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.

Ars staffers share their own reminiscences about Stewart and what he meant to them below.

Ken Fisher, founder and editor-in-chief:

I had the good fortune to literally bump into Sir Patrick Stewart outside Bond 45 in Midtown Manhattan (when it was on 45th Street). I was coming out of the restaurant with a couple of colleagues one evening when I turned right into him. When my eyes met his, I entered a state of total confusion. I knew he loved and even played Broadway, but it didn’t register why he was here, right next to me.

Fortunately, I recovered—but then, for some unknown reason, I said in a pirate voice, “Scuse muh, Capt’n!” But he didn’t miss a beat, smiled, and took a posture of “after you good sir!” I immediately chuckled like a fool and then added that I loved his work both on and off the stage. He thanked me, and we kept on rolling. I am thankful to this day that I didn’t say something corny like “two to beam up.”

What struck me about the exchange was that, as brief as it was, he did not appear annoyed in the slightest. And while I know he is a world-class actor, he also seemed genuinely appreciative of the comment. I am grateful today that I got to share my appreciation with him, awkward though it was.

Eric Berger, senior space editor:

Warmth. Humanity. Decency. Honesty. Integrity. Intellectualism. These are but a few of the traits I associate with Captain Jean-Luc Picard. At a time when our leadership in the United States, and many other countries around the world, regularly showcases the opposite of these characteristics, is it any wonder that we dearly miss the captain of theEnterprise-D? Picard first graced our TV screens in the late 1980s, a super impressionable time for me. As a result, for a time, that is how I expected most leaders would behave. Alas, no.

I’m sure everyone has their favorite Picard scenes, but for me it came at the very end ofThe Next Generation; we had all gotten to know and love the bridge crew so well, and it felt so bittersweet that it all was ending. There was Jean-Luc, who had maintained his professional distance for seven years, joining his crew at the poker table. And now, not just the series is over, but so too is the era in which Patrick Stewart was alive and making the world a better place. It’s a little darker outside.

Kyle Orland, senior gaming editor:

With Patrick Stewart’s death, there will be plenty of people remembering all of theStar Trek: The Next Generationmoments when he ably portrayed Captain Picard as the moral and diplomatic core of the show. And for sure, Stewart’s meaty and memorable monologues in episodes likeThe Drumhead,The First Duty,Darmok,Chain of Command, and more will be long remembered by sci-fi fans and studied by actors honing their craft.

But the most lasting Captain Picard moments for me are often the ones where Stewart got to let his hair down (so to speak) and show some rare emotional vulnerability in what was usually such a composed and professional character.

I’ll remember watching Picardwrestling with and crying to his brotherafter the trauma of being overtaken by the Borg, orchasing a dream-world grandson around on his hands and knees. I’ll remember the pain in Stewart’s eyes aftera psychic implant revealed his true feelings for Dr. Crusheror when he was forced to struggle withthe weight of sending a new romantic interest and subordinate on a dangerous mission. I’ll remember countless small moments like Picarddowning a shot of Aldebaran whiskeywith a time-shifted Scottie,being duly chagrined by a Captain Picard Day bannerduring a video call with an admiral, orpretending to be the barberwhile thwarting smugglers on an otherwise empty ship.

It’s these smaller emotional character moments—and Stewart’s ability to make so much of them—that added depth and roundness to Captain Picard’s character over the years. And that continued all the way up toNext Generation‘s very final moments, where Stewart captures the wistfulness and regret of Picard finally deciding to join the senior staff poker game. “Five card stud, nothing wild… and the sky’s the limit.”

Jeremy Hsu, technology reporter:

As a very casual Star Trek viewer, I only really began to grasp the depth of Patrick Stewart’s acting when I became enthralled by the silver screen chemistry between him and co-star Ian McKellen in the X-Men film franchise. The love-hate relationship and emotional vulnerability that Stewart and McKellen instilled in their roles as old-friends-turned-rivals has resonated with me throughout the years, and I still have deep appreciation for how the actors’ real-life friendship grew from that acting experience.

I also count myself extremely fortunate to have seen Stewart and McKellen perform together in a Broadway stage revival of the playWaiting for Godotin 2014. I’m sad they won’t be performing together again, but whenever they had the opportunity, they shone brightly indeed.

Jacob May, copy editor:

Hope and altruism are central themes in Stewart’s iconic roles, and they resonated most with me during one of my lowest moments.

Ever the one to inspire, Stewart’s role as Professor X in many X-Men films encouraged people and mutants to see the best in themselves and in each other. In 2014’sDays of Future Past, his pep talk extended to new ears: a younger, disillusioned version of himself (played by James McAvoy), and he may have well been speaking to me, too. Professor X’s telepathic abilities transcend space, time, and reality—don’t question it too much.

Upon the film’s release, I was freshly laid off from my hometown newspaper after the copy desk saw its numbers cut in half. (What was already a skeleton crew became less than that.) It wasn’t lost on me that being a cynic and malcontent was partly why I wasn’t picked to remain at the paper. In my late 20s, I questioned many of the decisions that set me on my journalism path, unsure what would happen to my career.

The younger Charles Xavier finds himself in a similar spot: angry with himself, with other people, and with the general state of things—and he’s seemingly out of a job. The older Professor X reminds his younger self that people can overcome their self-defeating flaws. “Just because someone stumbles and loses their way doesn’t mean they’re lost forever.”

Younger Chuck laments being tormented by people’s accounts of their pain, something a person who reads the news for a living can relate to. I try to unplug from Cerebro—er, my computer—when I’m off the clock. Xavier doesn’t have that luxury. The constant voices have driven him to despair and left him increasingly jaded.

But older Xavier calls him out, saying it’s his own mindset that’s holding him back. “We need you to hope again,” he says.

Therein lies the answer to Xavier’s malady: hope. And, as it turns out, the advice was also applicable to a young journalist in a crumbling industry. Incidentally, Stewart also found himself at a career crossroads as a young man, though he wasn’t too far along a chosen path,according to the Hollywood Reporter.

At 15, he got a job at the local newspaper, The Dewsbury Reporter, where he was tasked with interviewing bereaved family members when someone in town died. Journalism turned out not to be his passion, and he spent much of his free time with drama groups. His editor finally told him he had to choose between acting and journalism—and he quit on the spot.

Maybe if I had an Englishman’s commanding baritone, I would have made the same choice.

Ryan Whitwam, senior technology reporter:

Patrick Stewart was a prolific actor, but I will always associate him most with Jean-Luc Picard onStar Trek: The Next Generation, a show that made a real impression on me as a nerdy kid. It was refreshing to see a leader who valued science and reason—someone who didn’t immediately reach for their phaser. Despite the sometimes silly sci-fi subject matter, Stewart never seemed like he was too good to be spouting technobabble, even though he was famously skeptical of the role at first. Stewart’s portrayal of Picard elevated the series and helped it to age into a classic that I (and I’m sure many of you) still enjoy.

I also appreciate that he took so many different roles in movies and TV during his post-Trek career. Whenever I saw Patrick Stewart pop up on my screen or heard his voice unexpectedly come out of a cartoon character, it was a reminder of how happyTNGmade me over the years. I’ll miss that, and I’ll miss knowing that Patrick Stewart is out there being a kind, thoughtful guy off screen.

Lee Hutchinson, senior technology editor:

The version of Patrick Stewart that lives in my head will most often be the noble starship captain who taught uslife lessonsevery Friday night at 7 pm on channel 39. But while Stewart was obviously fantastic at portraying Picard’s stentorian and often stuffy formality, I was surprised when I discovered that the man behind the uniform was… surprisingly hilarious.

I tuned into his early 1994Saturday Night Liveappearance expecting an endless series ofTrekriffs, but what I got instead was a sketch aboutan erotic cake shoprun by a weirdly scatological baker. My confusion gave way to giggles—it was a one-note joke, but the image of Stewart in an apron talking about “sexy cakes” has stuck in my head for decades. He committed to it every bit as hard as he committed to following the Prime Directive, and at 16, it made me realize that anyone who could go from “The first duty of a Starfleet officer is to the truth!” tothatand sell them both with equal intensity and sincerity was not a one-note actor. This was a man with a hell of a lot of range!

The performance that brought me the most joy, though, washis turn on Ricky Gervais’Extras, where he played a version of himself as an actor, delivering career advice to Gervais. The scene is a masterclass in expectation subversion, something Stewart often seemed to revel in. I won’t spoil it for the two or three readers who still haven’t had the pleasure, but I will say that to this day my wife and I still say, “I’ve seen everything, I’ve seen it all!” at each other regularly in conversation.

Farewell, Sir Patrick. You gave us so much. Thank you.

Jason Marlin, technical director:

Like many Gen Xers, I grew up loving the originalStar Trekseries. ButThe Next Generationheld a special place in my heart. From the moment it premiered, I was captivated by the mind-bending concepts it explored. Jean-Luc Picard quickly became one of my favorite characters. I admired his intelligence, leadership, and moral integrity. He was the quintessential Starfleet captain, and he made balding cool in a way only Michael Jordan could rival.

Years later, I discovered what would become my favorite Patrick Stewart performance: his formidable portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge on Broadway and in the 1999 adaptation ofA Christmas Carol.

For me, the movie remains the definitive version of Dickens’ classic, and watching it has become a cherished family holiday tradition. During the COVID lockdowns, we eagerly tuned in to Stewart’s readings of Shakespeare, and of course, his solo multipart rendition ofA Christmas Carol. A roaring fire, some warm drinks, and his perfect Shakespearean accent made everything seem right with the world.

Sir Patrick Stewart will be greatly missed in the Marlin household.

Nick Indge, senior technology reporter:

Growing up in the US, raised by Brits, there was something quietly thrilling about seeing a Yorkshireman handed the captain’s chair. Better still, it madeTNGlegitimate in the eyes of my parents—a classically trained Shakespearean actor wouldn’t be involved in anything unserious, surely. As I came of age in 2000, there he was again as Professor X. Of course he was. Who else could it have possibly been? Beyond the roles, though, he just seemed to be a genuinely good man, the Mr. Rogers and Weird Al tier of human being. And when the world was upside down at the height of COVID, there he was, reading me a daily sonnet.

]]>

item.title: Flesh-eating screwworms spread to third state and are attacking pets
item.description:
USDA has identified 74 animal cases in US since parasitic flies invaded in June.

For a genuine fright this Halloween, you can turn your gaze to the southern border, where ravenous, flesh-eating maggots are festering and have taken to eating people’s pets.

This week, the country’s New World Screwworm (NWS) infestation spread to a third state, Arizona, which joins New Mexico and Texas in being plagued by the horrifying parasites. To date,74 animal caseshave been identified in the US since the flies re-invaded the country in June.

The flies lay hundreds of eggs in wounds and moist orifices of animals, and the resulting voracious maggots feast on their victims. The maggots resemble screws and tortuously bore and twist into living flesh, causing severe, sometimes fatal wounds, before dropping to the ground to develop into adults.

Because of their ability to ravage livestock, the flies were eliminated from the country in the 1960s through aerial releases of sterile male flies, which thwart successful breeding. For years, they were held at bay using a biological barrier along the Darién Gap at the border of Panama and Colombia. But the barrier was breached in 2022, and the flies have made their way back to the US through Central America.

While they are largely seen as a threat to the livestock industry, they can also devastate wildlife, domestic pets, and in rarer cases,humans. According tothe latest datafromMexico’s Ministry of Health, the country has confirmed 806 cases of human screwworm infestations since the flies reemerged. Nine people died from the savage maggots.

In the US, most of the 74 confirmed cases have been in livestock. But some of the cases have been in domestic pets, mainly dogs. Just this week, the US Department of Agriculture recorded four new cases in domestic dogs—which includes the new detection in Arizona—as well as a domestic cat in New Mexico. That brings the pet total to 10 cases since the flies reemerged. The US has also detected one case in a wild elk, which was reported last week.

Arizona’s agriculture department said this week that the state’s index case was identified in a dog in Cochise County, which borders both New Mexico and Mexico. A local veterinarian examined the poor pup on October 26 and found a wound on the canine’s back that was “heavily infested with maggots consistent with NWS characteristics.”

“We remain prepared and vigilant, and we urge all livestock owners, pet owners, and other animal industry partners to continue to monitor animals closely and report any unusual wounds consistent with NWS immediately,” thestate said in an announcement.

The USDAconfirmed the infectionand said it was working closely with Arizona on a joint response to the expanded infestation.

item.title: Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death
item.description:
The space agency solicited ideas for reboosting Hubble four years ago, but they didn’t go anywhere.

The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century.

NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space ShuttleColumbiavisited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope’s orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction.

The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies’ current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope’s performance through, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry.

“The requirement includes that the boost and/or servicing mission must not harm the HST and that this mission is expected to occur by 2032,” NASA wrote in the RFI. The contractor would be responsible for providing the launch vehicle, servicing spacecraft, mission operations, and “crew if applicable.”

NASA is not committing to buying a Hubble rescue mission, but officials want to know who might be interested in mounting such a mission, how much it would cost, and which companies would have a realistic shot at reaching Hubble before it falls out of orbit and burns up on reentry. Orbital dynamicists currently predict that it will likely happen in 2033 or 2034 without intervention, but reentry forecasts can change based on solar activity.

It took 24 years for Hubble, which lacks onboard propulsion, to glide from its 2002 altitude of 362 miles (583 km) to its current orbit some 292 miles (470 km) above Earth. A reboost to NASA’s requirement of 373 miles (600 km) would likely keep Hubble in orbit for at least 25 more years.

You’ll be forgiven if you’ve heard this before. Jared Isaacman, a billionaire commercial astronaut, approached NASA in 2022 about a servicing mission to Hubble with a team of astronauts on SpaceX’s Dragon spacecraft. He proposed funding most of the mission, which would have reboosted Hubble by at least 30 miles (50 km). Engineers also studied using Dragon to attach a rescue pod onto Hubble with new gyroscopes to overcome problems with the telescope’sdebilitated pointing system.

NASA also released an RFI in 2022 for other teams to share how they might boost Hubble’s orbit. The agency received eight responses, including a joint robotic reboost proposal from Astroscale and Momentus to pair their satellite servicing technology and in-space transport capabilities.

Agency officials announced in 2024 they would pursue a reboost mission after reviewing the responses. Mark Clampin, the head of NASA’s astrophysics division at the time, said the servicing plans from Isaacman and SpaceX “were really just notional concepts.”

Fast forward to 2026. Isaacman is now NASA administrator, and the satellite servicing industry is maturing. Northrop Grumman launched the world’s most sophisticated robotic servicing satellite earlier this year in a partnership with DARPA, the Pentagon’s research and development agency. Smaller startups like Astroscale andStarfish Spacehave contracts for servicing and refueling demos with the US Space Force and NASA.

So it’s not unrealistic to think the commercial industry could reboost and service Hubble by 2032, given enough time and resources. That was one of the lessons learned from NASA’s last-minute bid to rescue one of its smaller space telescopes, named Swift, from an impending reentry.

NASA awarded a $30 million contract to a startup named Katalyst Space Technologies last year and gave the company just nine months to develop a mission to fly up to Swift, grab onto it, and propel it to a higher orbit, extending its useful lifetime. Remarkably, Katalyst built a rescue satellite and launched it by the deadline, and got within about 6 miles (10 km) of Swift. Ground teamsdecided not to move closerafter problems with Katalyst’s power and reaction control systems.

The Swift rescue attempt showed a servicing mission doesn’t have to cost billions of dollars, asone of NASA’s now-canceled servicing demo projectswas predicted to cost. But Hubble is a significantly more expensive asset than Swift, so if NASA goes forward with a rescue mission, the agency would like to give a contractor more than $30 million and nine months.

NASA does currently not have any funding allocated to procuring a Hubble reboost or servicing mission.

“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” Isaacman said in a NASA statement. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the Universe.”

A crewed servicing mission like the one Isaacman envisioned in 2022 is unlikely to happen now. SpaceX aims to retire its Crew Dragon fleet by 2030. In a post on X, Isaacman wrote that he expects the new RFI will “draw interest from robotics companies.”

NASA’s newer flagship observatories, sometimes described as successors to Hubble, are not actually one-for-one replacements. Hubble is tuned to observe the Universe in visible and ultraviolet light, while the Webb and Roman telescopes peer deeper into the infrared Universe. Astronomers will likely have to wait for the launch of NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory in the 2040s for an improvement on Hubble’s visible and ultraviolet vision.

“Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing,” said Nicky Fox, NASA’s associate administrator for science. “Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated reentry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.”
